title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: On the Real and Nominal Price of Commodities, or Their Price in Labour and Their Price in Money.

Every person is rich or poor depending on how far he can afford to enjoy the necessities, comforts, and pleasures of human life. But once the division of labour has fully taken hold, a man's own labour can supply him with only a very small part of these things. By far the greater part he has to get from the labour of other people, and he is rich or poor according to the quantity of that labour which he can command, or which he can afford to buy. The value of any commodity, then, to the person who owns it and who does not mean to use or consume it himself but to trade it for other commodities, is equal to the quantity of labour it lets him buy or command. Labour, therefore, is the real measure of the exchangeable value of all commodities.

The real price of anything—what it really costs the man who wants to acquire it—is the toil and trouble of acquiring it. What anything is really worth to the man who has acquired it and wants to dispose of it, or trade it for something else, is the toil and trouble it can spare him and can impose on other people. Whatever is bought with money, or with goods, is paid for by labour just as much as what we get through the exertion of our own bodies. That money, or those goods, do indeed save us this toil. They contain the value of a certain quantity of labour, which we exchange for what is at the time assumed to contain the value of an equal quantity. Labour was the first price, the original purchase money paid for all things. It was not by gold or silver, but by labour, that all the wealth of the world was originally bought; and its value, to those who own it and want to trade it for some new products, is exactly equal to the quantity of labour it can enable them to buy or command.

Wealth, as Mr Hobbes says, is power. But the person who either earns or inherits a great fortune does not necessarily gain or inherit any political power, whether civil or military. His fortune may perhaps give him the means of acquiring both; but merely owning that fortune does not automatically convey either to him. The power that owning it immediately and directly conveys to him is the power to purchase a certain command over all the labour, or over all the produce of labour, that is then in the market. His fortune is greater or smaller exactly in proportion to the extent of this power—that is, to the quantity of other men's labour, or, what amounts to the same thing, of the produce of other men's labour, which it enables him to buy or command. The exchangeable value of everything must always be exactly equal to the extent of the power it conveys to its owner.

But although labour is the real measure of the exchangeable value of all commodities, it is not the measure by which their value is usually estimated. It is often difficult to determine the ratio between two different quantities of labour. The time spent on two different kinds of work will not by itself always settle this ratio. The different degrees of hardship endured, and of skill exercised, must also be taken into account. There may be more labour in an hour of hard work than in two hours of easy business; or in an hour spent practising a trade that took ten years to learn than in a month of effort at an ordinary, undemanding job. But it is not easy to find any accurate measure of either hardship or skill. In trading the various products of different kinds of labour for one another, some allowance is in fact commonly made for both. It is adjusted, however, not by any precise measure, but by the haggling and bargaining of the market, according to that sort of rough equality which, though not exact, is good enough for carrying on the business of everyday life.

Besides, every commodity is more often traded for, and so compared with, other commodities than with labour. It is therefore more natural to estimate its exchangeable value by the quantity of some other commodity than by the quantity of labour it can produce. Most people, too, understand better what is meant by a quantity of a particular commodity than by a quantity of labour. The one is a plain, tangible thing; the other an abstract idea, which, though it can be made clear enough, is not quite so natural and obvious.

But once barter ceases and money becomes the common instrument of trade, every particular commodity is more often traded for money than for any other commodity. The butcher seldom carries his beef or mutton to the baker or the brewer in order to trade them for bread or beer; instead he carries them to the market, where he trades them for money, and afterwards trades that money for bread and beer. The amount of money he gets for them also governs the quantity of bread and beer he can afterwards buy. So it is more natural and obvious for him to estimate their value by the quantity of money—the commodity for which he immediately trades them—than by the quantity of bread and beer, the commodities for which he can trade them only through the go-between of another commodity; and rather to say that his butcher's meat is worth three-pence or four-pence a pound than that it is worth three or four pounds of bread, or three or four quarts of small beer. So it comes about that the exchangeable value of every commodity is more often estimated by the quantity of money than by the quantity of labour or of any other commodity that can be got in exchange for it.

Gold and silver, however, like every other commodity, vary in their value; they are sometimes cheaper and sometimes dearer, sometimes easier and sometimes harder to buy. The quantity of labour that any particular quantity of them can buy or command, or the quantity of other goods it will trade for, always depends on the richness or poverty of the mines that happen to be known around the time such exchanges are made. The discovery of the abundant mines of America reduced, in the sixteenth century, the value of gold and silver in Europe to about a third of what it had been before. Since it took less labour to bring those metals from the mine to the market, so, once brought there, they could buy or command less labour; and this revolution in their value, though perhaps the greatest, is by no means the only one that history records. But just as a measure of quantity—such as the natural foot, fathom, or handful, which is continually varying in its own size—can never be an accurate measure of the quantity of other things, so a commodity that is itself continually varying in its own value can never be an accurate measure of the value of other commodities. Equal quantities of labour may be said, at all times and places, to be of equal value to the labourer. In his ordinary state of health, strength, and spirits, and at his ordinary level of skill and dexterity, he must always lay down the same portion of his ease, his liberty, and his happiness. The price he pays must always be the same, whatever the quantity of goods he gets in return for it. Of these, indeed, it may sometimes buy a greater and sometimes a smaller quantity; but it is the value of the goods that varies, not that of the labour which buys them. At all times and places, that is dear which is hard to come by, or which costs much labour to acquire; and that is cheap which can be had easily, or with very little labour. Labour alone, therefore, never varying in its own value, is alone the ultimate and real standard by which the value of all commodities can at all times and places be estimated and compared. It is their real price; money is only their nominal price.

But although equal quantities of labour are always of equal value to the labourer, yet to the person who employs him they appear sometimes to be of greater and sometimes of smaller value. He buys them sometimes with a greater and sometimes with a smaller quantity of goods, and to him the price of labour seems to vary like that of everything else. It appears dear to him in the one case and cheap in the other. In reality, however, it is the goods that are cheap in the one case and dear in the other.

In this ordinary sense, then, labour, like commodities, may be said to have a real and a nominal price. Its real price may be said to consist in the quantity of the necessities and comforts of life given for it; its nominal price, in the quantity of money. The labourer is rich or poor, well or badly rewarded, in proportion to the real, not the nominal, price of his labour.

The distinction between the real and the nominal price of commodities and labour is not a matter of mere theory, but may sometimes be of considerable practical use. The same real price is always of the same value; but because of the variations in the value of gold and silver, the same nominal price is sometimes of very different values. So when a landed estate is sold subject to a perpetual rent, if it is intended that this rent should always be of the same value, it matters to the family in whose favour it is reserved that it should not be fixed as a particular sum of money. Its value would in that case be liable to variations of two different kinds: first, those arising from the different quantities of gold and silver contained at different times in coin of the same denomination; and second, those arising from the different values of equal quantities of gold and silver at different times.

Princes and sovereign states have frequently imagined that they had a short-term interest in reducing the quantity of pure metal contained in their coins; but they have seldom imagined that they had any interest in increasing it. The quantity of metal contained in the coins of all nations, I believe, has accordingly been almost continually decreasing, and hardly ever increasing. Such variations, therefore, tend almost always to lower the value of a money rent.

The discovery of the mines of America lowered the value of gold and silver in Europe. This decline, it is commonly supposed—though I suspect without any certain proof—is still going on gradually, and is likely to continue for a long time. On that assumption, then, such variations are more likely to lower than to raise the value of a money rent, even if it were stipulated to be paid not in such a quantity of coined money of such a denomination (in so many pounds sterling, for example), but in so many ounces, either of pure silver or of silver of a certain standard.

Rents that have been reserved in corn have kept their value much better than those reserved in money, even where the denomination of the coin has not been altered. By the 18th of Elizabeth it was enacted that a third of the rent of all college leases should be reserved in corn, to be paid either in kind or according to the current prices at the nearest public market. The money arising from this corn rent, though originally only a third of the whole, is, in the present day, according to Dr Blackstone, commonly close to double what arises from the other two-thirds. The old money rents of colleges must, by this account, have sunk to almost a fourth of their ancient value, or are worth little more than a fourth of the corn they were formerly worth. But since the reign of Philip and Mary the denomination of the English coin has undergone little or no alteration, and the same number of pounds, shillings, and pence has contained very nearly the same quantity of pure silver. This decline, therefore, in the value of the money rents of colleges has come entirely from the decline in the price of silver.

When the decline in the value of silver is combined with a reduction in the quantity of it contained in coin of the same denomination, the loss is frequently even greater. In Scotland, where the denomination of the coin has undergone much greater alterations than it ever did in England, and in France, where it has undergone still greater than it ever did in Scotland, some ancient rents, originally of considerable value, have in this way been reduced almost to nothing.

Equal quantities of labour will, at widely separated times, be bought more nearly with equal quantities of corn—the labourer's subsistence—than with equal quantities of gold and silver, or perhaps of any other commodity. Equal quantities of corn, therefore, will at widely separated times be more nearly of the same real value, or enable their owner to buy or command more nearly the same quantity of other people's labour. They will do this, I say, more nearly than equal quantities of almost any other commodity; for even equal quantities of corn will not do it exactly. The labourer's subsistence, or the real price of labour, as I shall try to show later, is very different on different occasions; more generous in a society advancing toward wealth than in one that is standing still, and in one that is standing still than in one that is going backwards. Every other commodity, however, will at any particular time buy a greater or smaller quantity of labour in proportion to the quantity of subsistence it can buy at that time. A rent reserved in corn, therefore, is liable only to the variations in the quantity of labour that a certain quantity of corn can buy. But a rent reserved in any other commodity is liable not only to the variations in the quantity of labour that a particular quantity of corn can buy, but also to the variations in the quantity of corn that can be bought by a particular quantity of that commodity.

It should be noted, however, that although the real value of a corn rent varies much less from century to century than that of a money rent, it varies much more from year to year. The money price of labour, as I shall try to show later, does not fluctuate from year to year with the money price of corn, but seems to be everywhere adjusted not to the temporary or occasional price of that necessity of life, but to its average or ordinary price. The average or ordinary price of corn, again, is governed, as I shall also try to show later, by the value of silver—by the richness or poverty of the mines that supply the market with that metal, or by the quantity of labour that must be employed, and consequently of corn that must be consumed, in order to bring a particular quantity of silver from the mine to the market. But the value of silver, though it sometimes varies greatly from century to century, seldom varies much from year to year, and frequently stays the same, or very nearly the same, for half a century or a century at a stretch. The ordinary or average money price of corn, therefore, may over so long a period stay the same, or very nearly the same, and along with it the money price of labour, provided at least that the society remains in other respects in the same, or nearly the same, condition. Meanwhile, the temporary and occasional price of corn may frequently be double in one year of what it was the year before, fluctuating, for example, from twenty-five to fifty shillings the quarter. But when corn is at the latter price, not only the nominal but the real value of a corn rent will be double of what it is at the former, or will command double the quantity either of labour or of most other commodities; the money price of labour, and with it that of most other things, staying the same throughout all these fluctuations.

Labour, then, it plainly appears, is the only universal as well as the only accurate measure of value, the only standard by which we can compare the values of different commodities at all times and in all places. We cannot, it is granted, estimate the real value of different commodities from century to century by the quantities of silver given for them. We cannot estimate it from year to year by the quantities of corn. By the quantities of labour, we can estimate it with the greatest accuracy, both from century to century and from year to year. From century to century, corn is a better measure than silver, because from century to century equal quantities of corn will command the same quantity of labour more nearly than equal quantities of silver. From year to year, on the contrary, silver is a better measure than corn, because equal quantities of it will more nearly command the same quantity of labour.

But although, in setting up perpetual rents, or even in granting very long leases, it may be useful to distinguish between real and nominal price, it is of no use in buying and selling, the more common and ordinary transactions of human life.

At the same time and place, the real and the nominal price of all commodities are exactly in proportion to one another. The more or less money you get for any commodity in the London market, for example, the more or less labour it will at that time and place enable you to buy or command. At the same time and place, therefore, money is the exact measure of the real exchangeable value of all commodities. But it is so only at the same time and place.

Although at distant places there is no fixed proportion between the real and the money price of commodities, the merchant who carries goods from one to the other has nothing to consider but the money price—that is, the difference between the quantity of silver for which he buys them and that for which he is likely to sell them. Half an ounce of silver at Canton in China may command a greater quantity both of labour and of the necessities and comforts of life than an ounce at London. A commodity, therefore, that sells for half an ounce of silver at Canton may there be really dearer—of more real importance to the man who owns it there—than a commodity selling for an ounce at London is to the man who owns it at London. If a London merchant, however, can buy at Canton for half an ounce of silver a commodity he can afterwards sell at London for an ounce, he gains a hundred per cent by the bargain, just as much as if an ounce of silver were at London exactly of the same value as at Canton. It makes no difference to him that half an ounce of silver at Canton would have given him command of more labour, and of a greater quantity of the necessities and comforts of life, than an ounce can at London. An ounce at London will always give him command of double the quantity of all these things that half an ounce could have given there, and this is precisely what he wants.

Since it is the nominal or money price of goods, therefore, that finally decides the wisdom or folly of all purchases and sales, and so governs almost the whole business of everyday life in which price is concerned, it is no wonder that it should have been attended to so much more than the real price.

In a work like this, however, it may sometimes be useful to compare the different real values of a particular commodity at different times and places, or the different degrees of power over other people's labour that it may, on different occasions, have given to those who owned it. In this case we must compare, not so much the different quantities of silver for which it was commonly sold, as the different quantities of labour that those different quantities of silver could have bought. But the current prices of labour at distant times and places can scarcely ever be known with any degree of exactness. Those of corn, though they have been regularly recorded in few places, are in general better known and have been noted more often by historians and other writers. We must generally, therefore, content ourselves with them—not as being always in exactly the same proportion as the current prices of labour, but as being the nearest approximation that can commonly be had to that proportion. I shall later have occasion to make several comparisons of this kind.

As industry advanced, commercial nations found it convenient to coin several different metals into money: gold for larger payments, silver for purchases of moderate value, and copper, or some other coarse metal, for those of still smaller value. They have always, however, regarded one of those metals as more particularly the measure of value than either of the other two; and this preference seems generally to have been given to the metal they happened first to use as the instrument of trade. Having once begun to use it as their standard—which they must have done when they had no other money—they have generally continued to do so even when the necessity was no longer the same.

The Romans are said to have had nothing but copper money until within five years before the first Punic war (Pliny, book xxxiii, chapter 3), when they first began to coin silver. Copper, therefore, appears to have continued always the measure of value in that republic. At Rome all accounts seem to have been kept, and the value of all estates computed, either in asses or in sestertii. The as was always the denomination of a copper coin. The word sestertius means two asses and a half. So although the sestertius was originally a silver coin, its value was reckoned in copper. At Rome, a man who owed a great deal of money was said to have a great deal of other people's copper.

The northern nations that established themselves on the ruins of the Roman empire seem to have had silver money from the very beginning of their settlements, and not to have known either gold or copper coins for several ages afterwards. There were silver coins in England in the time of the Saxons; but little gold was coined until the time of Edward III, nor any copper until that of James I of Great Britain. In England, therefore—and for the same reason, I believe, in all the other modern nations of Europe—all accounts are kept, and the value of all goods and of all estates is generally computed, in silver; and when we mean to express the size of a person's fortune, we seldom mention the number of guineas, but the number of pounds sterling we suppose would be given for it.

Originally, in all countries, I believe, a legal tender of payment could be made only in the coin of the metal that was particularly regarded as the standard or measure of value. In England, gold was not regarded as legal tender for a long time after it was coined into money. The ratio between the values of gold and silver money was not fixed by any public law or proclamation, but was left to be settled by the market. If a debtor offered payment in gold, the creditor might either refuse such payment altogether or accept it at whatever valuation of the gold he and his debtor could agree on. Copper is not at present legal tender, except in making change for the smaller silver coins.
In this state of things, the distinction between the metal that was the standard and the metal that was not was something more than a merely nominal distinction.

In time, as people gradually became more familiar with the use of the different metals in coin, and so better acquainted with the ratio between their respective values, it has in most countries, I believe, been found convenient to fix this ratio and to declare by a public law that a guinea, for example, of such a weight and fineness should exchange for twenty-one shillings, or be legal tender for a debt of that amount. In this state of things, and so long as any one regulated ratio of this kind continues, the distinction between the metal that is the standard and the metal that is not becomes little more than a nominal distinction.

As a result of any change, however, in this regulated ratio, this distinction becomes—or at least seems to become—something more than nominal again. If the regulated value of a guinea, for example, were either reduced to twenty or raised to twenty-two shillings, then, since all accounts are kept and almost all debt obligations expressed in silver money, the greater part of payments could in either case be made with the same quantity of silver money as before, but would require very different quantities of gold money—more in the one case, less in the other. Silver would appear more invariable in its value than gold. Silver would appear to measure the value of gold, and gold would not appear to measure the value of silver. The value of gold would seem to depend on the quantity of silver it would exchange for, and the value of silver would not seem to depend on the quantity of gold it would exchange for. This difference, however, would be entirely due to the custom of keeping accounts, and of expressing the amount of all sums large and small, in silver rather than in gold money. One of Mr Drummond's notes for twenty-five or fifty guineas would, after an alteration of this kind, still be payable with twenty-five or fifty guineas, just as before. After such an alteration it would be payable with the same quantity of gold as before, but with very different quantities of silver. In the payment of such a note, gold would appear more invariable in its value than silver. Gold would appear to measure the value of silver, and silver would not appear to measure the value of gold. If the custom of keeping accounts, and of expressing promissory notes and other money obligations, in this manner were ever to become general, gold, and not silver, would be regarded as the metal that was particularly the standard or measure of value.

In reality, so long as any one regulated ratio between the respective values of the different metals in coin continues, the value of the most precious metal governs the value of the whole coinage. Twelve copper pence contain half a pound avoirdupois of copper, of not the best quality, which before it is coined is seldom worth seven-pence in silver. But because, by the regulation, twelve such pence are required to exchange for a shilling, they are in the market treated as worth a shilling, and a shilling can at any time be had for them. Even before the recent reform of the gold coin of Great Britain, the gold—at least the part of it that circulated in London and its neighbourhood—was in general less degraded below its standard weight than the greater part of the silver. Twenty-one worn and defaced shillings, however, were treated as equivalent to a guinea, which perhaps was itself worn and defaced too, but seldom so much. The recent regulations have brought the gold coin as near to its standard weight, perhaps, as it is possible to bring the current coin of any nation; and the order to receive no gold at the public offices except by weight is likely to keep it so, as long as that order is enforced. The silver coin still remains in the same worn and degraded state as before the reform of the gold coin. In the market, however, twenty-one shillings of this degraded silver coin are still treated as worth a guinea of this excellent gold coin.
The reform of the gold coin has evidently raised the value of the silver coin that can be exchanged for it.

In the English mint, a pound weight of gold is coined into forty-four and a half guineas, which at twenty-one shillings to the guinea is equal to forty-six pounds fourteen shillings and sixpence. An ounce of such gold coin, therefore, is worth £3 17s 10½d in silver. In England no duty or seignorage is paid on the coinage, and a man who carries a pound weight or an ounce weight of standard gold bullion to the mint gets back a pound weight or an ounce weight of gold in coin, without any deduction. Three pounds seventeen shillings and tenpence halfpenny an ounce, therefore, is said to be the mint price of gold in England—that is, the quantity of gold coin the mint gives in return for standard gold bullion.

Before the reform of the gold coin, the market price of standard gold bullion had for many years been above £3 18s, sometimes £3 19s, and very frequently £4 an ounce; and that sum, in the worn and degraded gold coin, probably seldom contained more than an ounce of standard gold. Since the reform of the gold coin, the market price of standard gold bullion seldom exceeds £3 17s 7d an ounce. Before the reform of the gold coin, the market price was always more or less above the mint price. Since that reform, the market price has been constantly below the mint price. But that market price is the same whether it is paid in gold or in silver coin. The recent reform of the gold coin, therefore, has raised not only the value of the gold coin but likewise that of the silver coin in proportion to gold bullion, and probably too in proportion to all other commodities; though, since the price of most other commodities is influenced by so many other causes, the rise in the value of either gold or silver coin in proportion to them may not be so distinct and noticeable.

In the English mint, a pound weight of standard silver bullion is coined into sixty-two shillings, containing, in the same way, a pound weight of standard silver. Five shillings and twopence an ounce, therefore, is said to be the mint price of silver in England—that is, the quantity of silver coin the mint gives in return for standard silver bullion. Before the reform of the gold coin, the market price of standard silver bullion was, on different occasions, five shillings and fourpence, five shillings and fivepence, five shillings and sixpence, five shillings and sevenpence, and very often five shillings and eightpence an ounce. Five shillings and sevenpence, however, seems to have been the most common price. Since the reform of the gold coin, the market price of standard silver bullion has fallen occasionally to five shillings and threepence, five shillings and fourpence, and five shillings and fivepence an ounce, the last of which it has scarcely ever exceeded. Although the market price of silver bullion has fallen considerably since the reform of the gold coin, it has not fallen as low as the mint price.

In the ratio between the different metals in the English coin, just as copper is rated far above its real value, so silver is rated somewhat below it. In the market of Europe—in the French coin and in the Dutch coin—an ounce of fine gold exchanges for about fourteen ounces of fine silver. In the English coin it exchanges for about fifteen ounces, that is, for more silver than it is worth according to the common reckoning of Europe. But just as the price of copper in bars is not, even in England, raised by the high price of copper in English coin, so the price of silver in bullion is not lowered by the low rate of silver in English coin. Silver in bullion still keeps its proper proportion to gold, for the same reason that copper in bars keeps its proper proportion to silver.

On the reform of the silver coin in the reign of William III, the price of silver bullion still continued to be somewhat above the mint price. Mr Locke attributed this high price to the permission to export silver bullion and the prohibition against exporting silver coin. This permission to export, he said, made the demand for silver bullion greater than the demand for silver coin. But the number of people who want silver coin for the common purposes of buying and selling at home is surely much greater than the number who want silver bullion either for export or for any other use. There exists at present a similar permission to export gold bullion, and a similar prohibition against exporting gold coin; and yet the price of gold bullion has fallen below the mint price. But in the English coin, silver was then, just as now, under-rated in proportion to gold; and the gold coin (which at that time too was not supposed to need any reform) governed then, as well as now, the real value of the whole coinage. Since the reform of the silver coin did not then reduce the price of silver bullion to the mint price, it is not very likely that a similar reform would do so now.

If the silver coin were brought back as near to its standard weight as the gold, a guinea, by the present ratio, would probably exchange for more silver in coin than it would buy in bullion. Since the silver coin would then contain its full standard weight, there would in that case be a profit in melting it down, in order first to sell the bullion for gold coin, and afterwards to exchange this gold coin for silver coin, to be melted down in the same way. Some alteration in the present ratio seems to be the only way of preventing this drawback.

The drawback, perhaps, would be less if silver were rated in the coin as much above its proper proportion to gold as it is at present rated below it, provided it were at the same time enacted that silver should not be legal tender for more than the change of a guinea—just as copper is not legal tender for more than the change of a shilling. No creditor could in that case be cheated by the high valuation of silver in coin, just as no creditor can at present be cheated by the high valuation of copper. The bankers alone would suffer by this regulation. When there is a run on them, they sometimes try to gain time by paying in sixpences, and this regulation would shut them out from this discreditable method of putting off immediate payment. They would consequently be obliged to keep at all times a greater quantity of cash in their coffers than at present; and though this might no doubt be a considerable inconvenience to them, it would at the same time be a considerable security to their creditors.

Three pounds seventeen shillings and tenpence halfpenny (the mint price of gold) certainly does not contain, even in our present excellent gold coin, more than an ounce of standard gold, and it might be thought, therefore, that it should not buy more standard bullion. But gold in coin is more convenient than gold in bullion; and although in England the coinage is free, yet the gold carried in bullion to the mint can seldom be returned in coin to the owner until after a delay of several weeks. In the present rush at the mint, it could not be returned until after a delay of several months. This delay is equivalent to a small duty, and makes gold in coin somewhat more valuable than an equal quantity of gold in bullion. If, in the English coin, silver were rated according to its proper proportion to gold, the price of silver bullion would probably fall below the mint price, even without any reform of the silver coin; the value even of the present worn and defaced silver coin being governed by the value of the excellent gold coin for which it can be exchanged.

A small seignorage or duty on the coinage of both gold and silver would probably increase still further the superiority of those metals in coin over an equal quantity of either of them in bullion. The coinage would in that case increase the value of the metal coined in proportion to the size of this small duty, for the same reason that the workmanship increases the value of plate in proportion to the cost of that workmanship. The superiority of coin over bullion would prevent the melting down of the coin, and would discourage its export. If, on any public emergency, it should become necessary to export the coin, the greater part of it would soon return again of its own accord. Abroad, it could sell only for its weight in bullion. At home, it would buy more than that weight. There would be a profit, therefore, in bringing it home again. In France, a seignorage of about eight per cent is imposed on the coinage, and the French coin, when exported, is said to return home again of its own accord.

The occasional fluctuations in the market price of gold and silver bullion arise from the same causes as the like fluctuations in the price of all other commodities. The frequent loss of those metals through various accidents by sea and by land, the continual waste of them in gilding and plating, in lace and embroidery, in the wear and tear of coin and of plate, all require, in every country that has no mines of its own, a continual importation in order to repair this loss and waste. The importing merchants, like all other merchants, we may believe, try as best they can to match their occasional imports to what they judge is likely to be the immediate demand. With all their care, however, they sometimes overdo it and sometimes underdo it. When they import more bullion than is wanted, rather than run the risk and trouble of exporting it again they are sometimes willing to sell part of it for something less than the ordinary or average price. When, on the other hand, they import less than is wanted, they get something more than this price. But when, despite all these occasional fluctuations, the market price of either gold or silver bullion continues for several years together steadily and constantly either more or less above, or more or less below, the mint price, we may be sure that this steady and constant superiority or inferiority of price is the effect of something in the state of the coin which at that time makes a certain quantity of coin either of more value or of less value than the precise quantity of bullion it ought to contain. The constancy and steadiness of the effect presupposes a corresponding constancy and steadiness in the cause.

The money of any particular country is, at any particular time and place, a more or less accurate measure of value, depending on how exactly the current coin conforms to its standard, or contains the precise quantity of pure gold or pure silver it ought to contain. If in England, for example, forty-four and a half guineas contained exactly a pound weight of standard gold, or eleven ounces of fine gold and one ounce of alloy, the gold coin of England would be as accurate a measure of the actual value of goods at any particular time and place as the nature of the thing would allow. But if, by rubbing and wearing, forty-four and a half guineas generally contain less than a pound weight of standard gold—the reduction, moreover, being greater in some pieces than in others—the measure of value comes to be liable to the same sort of uncertainty to which all other weights and measures are commonly exposed. Since it rarely happens that these conform exactly to their standard, the merchant adjusts the price of his goods as well as he can, not to what those weights and measures ought to be, but to what, on an average, he finds by experience they actually are. As a result of a similar disorder in the coin, the price of goods comes in the same way to be adjusted not to the quantity of pure gold or silver the coin ought to contain, but to the quantity that, on an average, it is found by experience actually to contain.

By the money price of goods, it should be noted, I always understand the quantity of pure gold or silver for which they are sold, without any regard to the denomination of the coin. Six shillings and eightpence, for example, in the time of Edward I, I regard as the same money price as a pound sterling in the present day, because it contained, as nearly as we can judge, the same quantity of pure silver.
